Two Latent Class Variables: Association, Covariates and Moderation

Source: vignettes/joint_classes.Rmd
joint_classes.Rmd
library(mixtureEM)

Some research questions are about two typologies at once. Do the profiles of childhood adversity a survey finds go with the profiles of substance use it also finds? Is that link the same for girls and boys? Each typology is a latent class variable measured by its own items, and the question is about the association between the two. fit_joint_classes() fits both latent variables in one model, with the association written as a multinomial logistic regression of one on the other, the loglinear model with latent variables of Hagenaars (1993). Covariates can predict either variable, and a covariate’s effect on the second can differ across the classes of the first, which is how a moderated association is written.

What a latent class analysis is, and how to choose the number of classes, is in vignette("class_enumeration"); here each variable’s number of classes is taken as settled.

The data

The example is simulated, so that the answer is known. For 1,500 adolescents there are six yes/no items about adverse childhood experiences (a1 to a6) and five items about substance use, each answered never (1), sometimes (2) or often (3) (s1 to s5). Behind them are two latent variables with three classes each: adversity (x: low, household adversity, high) and substance use (y: abstains, drinks, several substances). High adversity goes with several substances, and being a girl lowers the odds of several substances, most of all after high adversity. Three answers in a hundred are missing at random.

set.seed(7070)
n <- 1500
female <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
# Adversity class: 1 low, 2 household, 3 high; girls a little more often 2.
lp <- cbind(0, -0.6 + 0.5 * female, -1.2)
cx <- apply(exp(lp) / rowSums(exp(lp)), 1, function(p) sample(1:3, 1, prob = p))
# Substance-use class given adversity: 1 abstains, 2 drinks, 3 several
# substances. Logits against class 1, by adversity class; being female lowers
# the odds of several substances, most of all after high adversity.
assoc <- rbind(c(0, -0.4, -2.2), c(0, 0.3, -0.6), c(0, 0.6, 0.9))
lc <- assoc[cx, ] + cbind(0, 0, -c(0.2, 0.4, 1.2)[cx] * female)
cy <- apply(exp(lc) / rowSums(exp(lc)), 1, function(p) sample(1:3, 1, prob = p))
# Six yes/no adversity items and five never/sometimes/often use items.
p_a <- rbind(c(.10, .08, .12, .05, .10, .06),
             c(.70, .65, .55, .20, .15, .10),
             c(.80, .75, .70, .65, .60, .55))
adversity <- matrix(rbinom(n * 6, 1, p_a[cx, ]), n, 6,
                    dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("a", 1:6)))
use_level <- rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0), c(2, 0, 1, 0, 0), c(2, 2, 2, 1, 1))
use <- matrix(NA_integer_, n, 5, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("s", 1:5)))
for (j in 1:5) {
  hi <- use_level[cy, j]
  r <- runif(n)
  use[, j] <- 1 + ifelse(hi == 0, (r > .80) + (r > .95),
              ifelse(hi == 1, (r > .30) + (r > .80), (r > .10) + (r > .40)))
}
adversity[runif(n * 6) < 0.03] <- NA
use[runif(n * 5) < 0.03] <- NA

cx and cy are the true classes the analysis will try to recover; a real analysis never has them. All it has is adversity, use and female.

One step or two

The model can be estimated in one step, every parameter at once, or in two (Bakk & Kuha, 2018). In two steps, step 1 fits each latent variable’s measurement model on its own, as two separate latent class analyses, and step 2 holds those item parameters fixed while it estimates the association and the covariate effects. The two-step estimator has a property that matters when several structural models are compared: the classes are defined by their own items only, so they mean the same thing in every model, and a covariate added in step 2 cannot change what a class is. Its standard errors include the uncertainty of step 1. The analysis below is two-step, with the one-step fit as a check at the end.

Every fit switches off the package’s default priors, which keep estimates away from the boundary and are the right default for exploratory work. Without them the fits are plain maximum likelihood, the estimator the two-step method and the likelihood-ratio tests below are defined for; vignette("estimation") explains what the priors add and when to keep them.

ml <- list(smoothing = 0, bayes_constants = list(categorical = 0))

The association with covariates

The first structural model has the association and female predicting both variables, its effect on y the same in every adversity class (y_effects = "common", the default).

fem <- data.frame(female = female)
m1 <- fit_joint_classes(adversity, use, n_x = 3, n_y = 3,
                        measurement_y = "ordinal",
                        predictors_x = fem, predictors_y = fem,
                        n_steps = 2, n_init = 20, random_state = 1,
                        smoothing = ml$smoothing,
                        bayes_constants = ml$bayes_constants)

Before the association, what the classes are. measurement_summary() gives each variable’s item profiles under its own classes, beside the observed share of each answer:

measurement_summary(m1)
#> =========================================================

These probabilities have run to 0 or 1, so the class is defined partly by an item every case in it gives the same answer to, and their standard errors are not interpretable. There are two ways on: read it substantively, since an item every member of a class answers identically is often the finding rather than a fault; or, if that parameter needs a standard error, refit with a stronger prior than the default of 1 - `bayes_constants = list(categorical = 2)` - which holds the estimate off the edge at the cost of shrinking it slightly toward the item's marginal.
#> =========================================================

The adversity classes are the three that were simulated: X#1 reports almost none of the six experiences, X#2 the first three (household adversity) and few of the rest, X#3 all six at around one half or more. The substance-use classes are too: Y#1 mostly answers never, Y#2 drinks often (s1) and sometimes uses the third substance, and Y#3 uses the first three substances often and the last two sometimes.

Four probabilities have run to 0 or 1, and the note under the tables says how to read them. The household class never reporting a6 is a finding about that class rather than a fault of the fit; it was simulated at 0.10, and in a class of a few hundred the estimate of a rare answer can be zero.

Now the association:

m1
#> Two latent class variables: x (3 classes, 6 items), y (3 classes, 5 items)
#> Log-likelihood -10499.379, 60 free parameters, BIC 21437.551
#> 
#> Two-step: item parameters fixed at the separate latent class analyses
#> 
#> Association: log-odds of y against its last class
#>    y      term   x estimate    se      z        p
#>  Y#1 Intercept      -0.0671 0.263 -0.255 7.98e-01
#>  Y#1       X#1 X#1   2.3990 0.344  6.964 3.31e-12
#>  Y#1       X#2 X#2   0.6601 0.404  1.634 1.02e-01
#>  Y#1    female       0.6574 0.221  2.979 2.89e-03
#>  Y#2 Intercept       0.6824 0.235  2.910 3.62e-03
#>  Y#2       X#1 X#1   1.4005 0.329  4.253 2.11e-05
#>  Y#2       X#2 X#2   0.0644 0.391  0.165 8.69e-01
#>  Y#2    female       0.5165 0.220  2.349 1.88e-02
#> 
#> Joint class probabilities P(x, y)
#>       Y#1   Y#2   Y#3
#> X#1 0.297 0.218 0.023
#> X#2 0.103 0.110 0.039
#> X#3 0.055 0.109 0.045
#> 
#> Conditional probabilities P(y | x)
#>       Y#1   Y#2   Y#3
#> X#1 0.552 0.405 0.042
#> X#2 0.408 0.436 0.156
#> X#3 0.264 0.522 0.215

Every log-odds is against the last class of each variable: Y#1 ON X#1 of 2.40 says that low adversity raises the odds of abstaining, rather than using several substances, by a factor of exp(2.40) = 11 compared with high adversity. The conditional probabilities say the same thing on the probability scale: 4% of the low-adversity class use several substances, 22% of the high-adversity class.

Is there an association at all?

The model with association = "none" holds the two variables independent given the covariates. Fitted on the same step 1 (step1 = m1), it is the restricted model of a likelihood-ratio test of the association, on (3 - 1) x (3 - 1) = 4 degrees of freedom.

m0 <- fit_joint_classes(adversity, use, n_x = 3, n_y = 3,
                        measurement_y = "ordinal",
                        predictors_x = fem, predictors_y = fem,
                        association = "none", n_steps = 2, step1 = m1,
                        smoothing = ml$smoothing,
                        bayes_constants = ml$bayes_constants)
lr_test(m0, m1)
#> 
#> Likelihood-ratio test for nested models
#> ---------------------------------------------------------
#>   Restricted : LL =  -10539.5218   parameters = 56
#>   Full       : LL =  -10499.3791   parameters = 60
#>   -2 x diff  : 80.2854   df = 4   p = 1.515e-16
#>   The restriction is rejected: the full model fits significantly better.

The two typologies are clearly associated.

Is the association the same for girls and boys?

y_effects = c(female = "by_x") lets the effect of female on substance use differ by adversity class. Against m1, that is a test of whether sex moderates the association, again on four degrees of freedom: one more slope per y logit for each adversity class but the last.

m2 <- fit_joint_classes(adversity, use, n_x = 3, n_y = 3,
                        measurement_y = "ordinal",
                        predictors_x = fem, predictors_y = fem,
                        y_effects = c(female = "by_x"),
                        n_steps = 2, step1 = m1,
                        smoothing = ml$smoothing,
                        bayes_constants = ml$bayes_constants)
lr_test(m1, m2)
#> 
#> Likelihood-ratio test for nested models
#> ---------------------------------------------------------
#>   Restricted : LL =  -10499.3791   parameters = 60
#>   Full       : LL =  -10494.5294   parameters = 64
#>   -2 x diff  : 9.6996   df = 4   p = 0.0458
#>   The restriction is rejected: the full model fits significantly better.

The moderation is significant at the 5% level, if not by much. The coefficients of a moderated model are hard to read directly (each female | X#k row is a difference from the last adversity class), so the result is best reported as the probabilities of each substance-use class given each adversity class, for boys and for girls. joint_probabilities() computes them at fixed covariate values, with delta-method standard errors:

boys  <- joint_probabilities(m2, at = list(female = 0))
girls <- joint_probabilities(m2, at = list(female = 1))
cbind(boys[, c("x", "y")], boys = round(boys$estimate, 3),
      girls = round(girls$estimate, 3))
#>     x   y  boys girls
#> 1 X#1 Y#1 0.525 0.590
#> 2 X#1 Y#2 0.428 0.373
#> 3 X#1 Y#3 0.047 0.037
#> 4 X#2 Y#1 0.344 0.447
#> 5 X#2 Y#2 0.510 0.396
#> 6 X#2 Y#3 0.146 0.157
#> 7 X#3 Y#1 0.283 0.245
#> 8 X#3 Y#2 0.400 0.662
#> 9 X#3 Y#3 0.317 0.092

After high adversity (X#3), 32% of boys are in the several-substances class and 9% of girls; after low adversity (X#1) both are under 5%. That is the moderation that was simulated: the link from adversity to using several substances is much stronger for boys.

Any other function of the coefficients, with its standard error, is available from derived_estimates(), using the parameter names joint_coefficients() documents.

The one-step fit as a check

The same three models in one step, every parameter estimated at once:

one <- lapply(list(m0 = "none", m1 = "common", m2 = "by_x"), function(s)
  fit_joint_classes(adversity, use, n_x = 3, n_y = 3,
                    measurement_y = "ordinal",
                    predictors_x = fem, predictors_y = fem,
                    association = if (s == "none") "none" else "free",
                    y_effects = if (s == "by_x") c(female = "by_x") else "common",
                    n_init = 20, random_state = 1, standard_errors = FALSE,
                    smoothing = ml$smoothing,
                    bayes_constants = ml$bayes_constants))
lr_test(one$m0, one$m1)
#> 
#> Likelihood-ratio test for nested models
#> ---------------------------------------------------------
#>   Restricted : LL =  -10539.1580   parameters = 56
#>   Full       : LL =  -10497.3270   parameters = 60
#>   -2 x diff  : 83.6620   df = 4   p = < 1e-16
#>   The restriction is rejected: the full model fits significantly better.
lr_test(one$m1, one$m2)
#> 
#> Likelihood-ratio test for nested models
#> ---------------------------------------------------------
#>   Restricted : LL =  -10497.3270   parameters = 60
#>   Full       : LL =  -10490.8376   parameters = 64
#>   -2 x diff  : 12.9788   df = 4   p = 0.01138
#>   The restriction is rejected: the full model fits significantly better.

The conclusions do not change: a strong association, and a moderation by sex that is significant at the 5% level. The one-step log-likelihoods are higher, as they must be, since step 1’s item parameters are free there; the price is that the classes’ meaning can shift a little from one structural model to the next.

Summary

  • fit_joint_classes() fits two latent class variables and their association in one model; measurement_summary() shows what each variable’s classes are.
  • association = "none" and y_effects = "by_x" give the restricted and the extended models of the two natural tests, run by lr_test().
  • With n_steps = 2, fit step 1 once and hand it to every structural model with step1 =, so that all of them share one measurement model.
  • Report a moderated association as conditional probabilities at chosen covariate values, with joint_probabilities().

References

Bakk, Z., & Kuha, J. (2018). Two-step estimation of models between latent classes and external variables. Psychometrika, 83(4), 871-892.

Hagenaars, J. A. (1993). Loglinear models with latent variables. Sage.
